You write an argumentative text of at least 250 words, well built and convincing, as in the DELF B2 writing paper.
Read the instructions carefully before writing.
Each paragraph develops a single idea.
You need at least two hundred and fifty words.
Know the format of the DELF B2 writing paper.
Analyse the topic: text type, addressee, register, central question.
Build a dialectical or thematic plan, with an introduction and a conclusion.
Write argumentative paragraphs: idea, explanation, example.
Proofread your text to remove agreement, conjugation and register errors.

Thursday, 11 December 2036, evening, in Julien’s kitchen. Two days to go before the exam. Inès, an eloquence champion and law student, explains to Haruka how to write an argumentative essay. Julien corrects the drafts.
First rule: you read the instructions three times. Who is writing? To whom? What for? An article, a letter, a forum post?
And what if I get the text type wrong?
You lose points, even if your French is perfect. A letter without a closing formula isn’t a letter.
Second rule: the rough draft. You take ten minutes to make a plan before writing a single sentence.
Ten minutes is a lot. The paper only lasts an hour.
That’s exactly why. Without a plan, you go round in circles. With a plan, the sentences come by themselves.
The safest: an introduction, two or three paragraphs, a conclusion. In each paragraph, an idea, an explanation, an example.
And don’t forget to nuance. Examiners love “certes… mais”. It shows you’ve thought about both sides.
And the two hundred and fifty words? Do I have to count them?
Yes. Count the words on one line, multiply by the number of lines. If you have fewer, you lose points. If you have three hundred, it doesn’t matter.
Last rule: keep ten minutes to reread. Agreements, accents, verbs. That’s where you win the last points.
Read, plan, write, reread. Like a score: you don’t play it without having read it.
The paper lasts one hour and is marked out of 25. You write a single argumentative text of at least 250 words:
a title, a clear thesis, arguments
a director, a mayor, a newspaper
a reaction to an opinion, arguments
Examiners mark: following the instructions, coherence, argumentation, vocabulary and grammar. Perfect French in a text that doesn’t answer the question gets a poor mark!
Who am I? Who am I writing to? (role, addressee)
What text type? What register? (usually standard to formal)
What is the central question? Rephrase it in your own words.
Dialectical plan: for / against / my opinion.
Typical mistake: writing straight onto the clean sheet. Without a plan, the text repeats itself, contradicts itself and never reaches a conclusion.
a hook, the central question, the announcement of the plan
De nos jours… On peut se demander si… Nous verrons d’abord… puis…
a summary of the ideas, your answer, an opening
En somme… Pour conclure… Il reste à savoir si…
Write the conclusion BEFORE rereading the whole text, so you don’t run out of time. A three-line conclusion is better than none.
Every paragraph has the same structure: IDEA → EXPLANATION → EXAMPLE.
IDEA: First, silence allows us to think better.
EXPLANATION: Indeed, it is hard to concentrate in noise.
EXAMPLE: For example, many students work in libraries.
Connectors for arguments: tout d’abord, de plus, en outre, par ailleurs, enfin. For explanations: en effet, car, c’est-à-dire. For concession: certes… mais, même si, bien que.
Reread TWICE: once for meaning (does it make sense?), once for grammar only (agreements, verbs, accents).
What do you do in the first minutes of the paper?
I read the instructions and make a plan in rough
I start the text straight away on the clean sheet
The structure of an argumentative paragraph:
Combien de fois faut-il lire la consigne, selon Inès ?
Combien de temps faut-il prendre pour le plan ?
Qu’est-ce que le correcteur adore, selon Julien ?
A letter without a closing formula…
In each paragraph: an idea, an explanation, an example.

Of all the papers, writing was the one that frightened Haruka most. She now understood the radio and read fast. But writing two hundred and fifty words in French, in an hour, without a dictionary, on a topic she would only discover on the day, seemed as hard as playing a sonata she had never seen, in front of a jury, without being allowed to stop. At the first writing mock exam, at the end of November, she got thirteen out of twenty-five.

The topic of that first mock exam was mass tourism. Haruka had plenty of ideas: she had seen the crowds in Kyoto in front of the temples and knew the problem well. She started writing straight away, without thinking, following her ideas in the order they came. After forty minutes she realised she had said the same thing three times in different words. She tried to conclude in five minutes. It showed.

The Alliance française teacher had handed back her paper covered in red. He had noted three problems. First, she hadn’t followed the instructions: they asked for a letter to a newspaper editor, and she had written an essay, with no salutation and no closing formula. Next, her text had no plan: the ideas repeated themselves and the conclusion came abruptly, as if she had run out of time. Finally, she had written only two hundred and ten words.

That evening she called Aoi in Kyoto. Aoi had studied calligraphy for ten years before musicology. She reminded her of a rule from her old master: the brush only touches the paper once the mind has seen the whole character. Whoever starts tracing without knowing where they’re going makes blots. Haruka said that was exactly what had happened to her: she had made blots. Aoi said: “Then look at the whole character first. Only then, write.”

Haruka showed the paper to Inès one evening on the landing. Inès read it in silence, very seriously, the way a lawyer reads a brief. Then she said Haruka’s French was good, very good even, better than half her law cohort’s. The problem wasn’t the language. It was the method. And method could be learnt in a week. Inès had won a national eloquence contest at sixteen. She knew what she was talking about.

She offered to coach her every evening, for an hour, until the exam. She called it “the Inès method”. It was simple. Every evening, one topic. Ten minutes to read the instructions and make a plan. Forty minutes to write. Ten minutes to reread. No more, no less. Rose-Hélène, who had insisted on taking part, held Amina’s kitchen timer. She took her role very seriously. She announced the time left every five minutes in a station master’s voice.

Inès was eighteen and in her first year of law. Her mother worked nights at the hospital, and Inès had learnt very early to manage on her own. She had started eloquence at secondary school by chance, because a teacher found her too chatty in class. Since then she had won contests, written a national op-ed defending Sami and organised the tree march in Lyon. Haruka found her impressive. Inès said she was mainly incapable of keeping quiet, except for eight bars.

On the first evening the topic was: “Should cars be banned from city centres? You are writing to the mayor of your town.” Haruka wanted to start writing straight away. Inès took the pen out of her hand. She asked her to read the instructions aloud three times and answer three questions. Who is writing? A resident. To whom? The mayor. What for? To persuade him. Haruka said that was already two minutes lost. Inès said they were the two most useful minutes of the hour.

Then she made her draw up a plan. Not sentences: words. One column for, one column against. Then she showed her how to turn those two columns into three paragraphs: advantages, disadvantages, a solution. On the draft she drew a diagram Haruka never forgot: a small rectangle for the introduction, three big rectangles for the paragraphs, a small rectangle for the conclusion. She said it was the skeleton of every argumentative text in the world.

In each big rectangle Inès wrote three words: idea, explanation, example. She said every paragraph had to follow that order, always. An idea, announced by a connector: “tout d’abord”, “de plus”, “enfin”. An explanation, often beginning with “en effet”. And a concrete example to bring the idea to life: “par exemple”, “ainsi”. Haruka said it was like a musical phrase: theme, development, cadence. Inès said she knew nothing about music, but it sounded right.

Rose-Hélène took her role as timekeeper with alarming rigour. She announced “thirty minutes”, then “twenty-five minutes”, then “twenty minutes, and this is no time for daydreaming”. One evening Haruka stopped to think about a word, eyes on the ceiling. Rose-Hélène said sternly: “Miss Mori, we write here, we don’t count flies.” Everyone burst out laughing. Inès said she had just found the best exam invigilator in France.

On the first evening Haruka wrote two hundred and thirty words in fifty minutes. The text was correct but flat. On the second, two hundred and sixty words, with a clear plan. On the third she got the text type wrong: they asked for a newspaper article with a title, and she had forgotten the title. Inès took off two imaginary points. On the fourth she wrote two hundred and eighty words, with a title, a plan, connectors and a conclusion. Inès said: “Now we can work.”

Julien took care of the corrections. Every evening after training he reread Haruka’s paper with a red pen, sitting at the kitchen table, glasses on the end of his nose. He underlined agreement errors, forgotten accents, badly conjugated verbs. He didn’t correct them himself: he underlined, and Haruka had to find the correction. He said that was how you learnt the piano: you don’t play in the pupil’s place, you show them where they went wrong.

Julien told her that Odile used to correct his letters. When he wrote to the town hall asking for a rehearsal room, or to the conservatoire about a post, he slipped the letter under the door opposite. The next morning it came back under his own door, with little pencil lines under the mistakes. Never corrections: just the lines. Odile said you remembered a mistake better if you had found it yourself. Julien said he did the same as her, with a red pen because he no longer had her pencil.

Haruka’s mistakes were always the same. She forgot to make adjectives agree with feminine nouns. She forgot to make the past participle agree when the object came before it. She confused “a” and “à”, “ou” and “où”. And she used the indicative after “il faut que”. Julien made a list of those five mistakes and stuck it on the first page of her notebook. He said that in the exam she should reread her paper looking only for those five mistakes. Nothing else.

Sami, who often dropped in at the rue d’Austerlitz after his literature classes, taught her something else: rhythm. He read one of her papers aloud and noticed that all her sentences were the same length. Subject, verb, object. Subject, verb, object. He said it was like music where every note lasted the same time. He showed her how to alternate a long sentence with a short one. He said a short sentence after a long one struck like a cymbal crash.

To show her, Sami recited a passage from his slam. A long sentence that climbed and climbed, with commas like steps on a staircase, and then, right at the top, three dry words: “And then, silence.” Haruka felt the difference physically, as when an orchestra stops dead after a crescendo. Sami said the best French writers had been doing that for centuries. They wrote with their ears as much as their heads. Haruka said that in that case she had an advantage. She had perfect pitch.

Haruka tried it that very evening. She wrote a long sentence about traffic jams, with two subordinate clauses and a well-placed comma. Then a short one: “The city is suffocating.” Sami read the two sentences aloud. He smiled. He said: “There. That’s a cymbal.” Haruka said it was the first time she had written a French sentence that rang. Sami said that was exactly what Hortense Valmont called having style. Haruka asked whether there were points for style. Sami said: “Not officially.”

Amina, of course, took care of the words. She taught Haruka her method for counting fast. You count the words on three lines, take the average, and multiply by the number of lines. She made a spreadsheet giving, for each handwriting, the number of lines needed to reach two hundred and fifty words. For Haruka’s small, regular handwriting, twenty-three were needed. Amina advised her to write twenty-eight, to be safe. She said a safety margin was the secret of every good spreadsheet.

The evening Amina presented her spreadsheet, Awa was sitting on her lap. She grabbed the sheet in her little hands and crumpled it with great enthusiasm before putting it in her mouth. Amina retrieved the sheet, slightly damp. She said Awa had a very clear opinion about safety margins. Bertrand said his daughter would no doubt become a Court of Auditors magistrate, since she could already destroy a spreadsheet in three seconds.

Bertrand, for his part, taught her formal letters. He had written thousands during his years at the Court of Auditors. He knew every formula by heart: “I am writing to you in order to…”, “I would be grateful if you would kindly…”, “Yours faithfully, Sir.” He explained that the closing formula had to echo the salutation exactly. “Madame” at the beginning, “Madame” at the end. Haruka found that very Japanese. Bertrand said it was above all very French.

Bertrand also told her about his worst mistake. Early in his career he had written a very important letter to a woman minister. He had put “Monsieur le Ministre” at the top, out of habit, because all ministers at the time were men. The minister replied with a two-line letter of icy politeness that began “Madame le Magistrat”. Bertrand said he had never forgotten the lesson: check the salutation before anything else. Haruka wrote the sentence in her notebook, in red.

On Wednesday an envelope arrived from Paris. It was Hortense Valmont. Inside was a sheet of cream paper written with a fountain pen in her fine, slanting hand. It was a list of connectors, sorted by function: to add, to contrast, to explain, to conclude. Thirty-six connectors in all. At the bottom of the page Hortense had written: “Don’t use more than ten. A text with too many connectors is like a house with too many doors. You no longer know where to come in.”

Haruka stuck the list next to Julien’s on the first page of her notebook. Then she reread Odile’s letters in the cardboard box. She noticed Odile almost never used connectors. Her sentences were simple and short, and yet everything flowed perfectly. Isabelle explained that this was the hardest thing: writing simply. Her mother had been a primary teacher for forty years. She said a complicated sentence often hid an idea you hadn’t properly understood.

On Wednesday evening Leïla, Sami’s mother, came by with honey cakes for the training sessions. She stayed a while. She said that when she arrived in France at twenty, she could hardly write French. She had learnt by writing letters for her neighbours in the tower who couldn’t write at all: letters to the benefits office, the school, the landlord. She said she had learnt official French before everyday French. Haruka said it was the bravest method she knew.

On Thursday evening Inès gave Haruka the last practice topic. She had chosen it carefully from dozens of past DELF papers. “Do you think social networks bring people together or drive them apart? You are writing an article for your university newspaper.” Haruka read the instructions three times. She answered the three questions. She made her plan in eight minutes. She wrote for forty minutes without stopping. She reread for twelve minutes, looking only for the five mistakes on Julien’s list.

She found four. She corrected them. Rose-Hélène announced the end of the hour in a solemn voice. Inès took the paper and read it in silence while everyone waited in the kitchen. Julien, Ioana, Isabelle, Sami, Rose-Hélène and Henri-Ion, who didn’t understand what was going on but sensed it was important. Inès put the paper down. She counted the words: three hundred and two. She said: “Nineteen out of twenty-five. Maybe twenty.” Henri-Ion clapped without knowing why.

On Thursday there was also orchestra rehearsal. Haruka wanted to skip it to work. Inès wouldn’t let her. She said she needed to rest her head, and nothing rested it better than music. At the end of rehearsal, Théo announced that that evening’s waltz was dedicated to Haruka. The whole orchestra played it for her. At the break, Bernard Delorme wished her luck, deliberately speaking very slowly, articulating every syllable. Haruka said she preferred it when he spoke fast. Bernard was very touched.

On Friday 12 December, the day before the exam, Isabelle forbade Haruka to work. No radio, no paper, no practice topic. She said musicians never rehearsed the day before a concert, and language was the same. You had to let it settle. They climbed up to Fourvière together, by the steps, to the white basilica that overlooks the city. It was very cold. The sky was grey and heavy. Isabelle said it was going to snow. Haruka had never seen snow in Lyon.

In the basilica, Isabelle lit a candle in front of a small side chapel. She said Odile lit one every year, on 8 December, for Henri, who was at sea. She wasn’t very religious, but she said the little flame helped sailors find their way home. Haruka lit a candle too. She wasn’t Catholic. But she thought of her grandmother in Kyoto and put her hands together in front of the flame, Japanese-style, for a long moment.

From the top of the hill you could see the whole city: the two rivers, the red roofs of Old Lyon, the Croix-Rousse on the other side, and in the distance, on a clear day, the Alps. Isabelle showed Haruka where the rue d’Austerlitz was, the Salle Hélène Morel, the Parc de la Tête d’Or, La Duchère. She said every important place in the story of the waltz was there before their eyes, within five kilometres. Haruka said that now she was part of it. Isabelle said: “Since the first day.”

That evening Ioana invited everyone to dinner at the rue d’Austerlitz, at her and Julien’s, on the other side of the landing. There were Isabelle, Haruka, Amina, Bertrand and Awa, Inès, Sami, and of course Rose-Hélène and Henri-Ion. Ioana had made sarmale, because she said it was the dish that brought luck before exams in Romania. Bertrand pointed out that in Romania, according to Ioana, sarmale brought luck before pretty much everything. Ioana said that was exactly why they worked.

During dinner Henri-Ion announced to everyone that he knew the date of the French Revolution, and shouted it: “Seventeen eighty-nine!” Haruka said she hoped she wouldn’t be asked that in the oral. Henri-Ion said that if she was, she only had to call him. Awa, in Bertrand’s arms, said “ba” very loudly in the middle of a silence. Amina asked whether that counted as a word. Bertrand said no. Amina recorded it anyway.

After dinner Ioana went to fetch something from a drawer. It was a yellowed envelope. Inside was a certificate: Ioana Popescu’s DELF B2, dated June 2027. She had taken it a year after arriving in Lyon, so she could work as an architect. Seventy-one out of a hundred. She said she had got seven out of twenty-five in the oral, nearly eliminated, because she panicked in front of the examiners. Haruka looked at the certificate for a long time. She said she hadn’t known Ioana had been afraid too.

Ioana smiled. She said everyone was afraid. Fear wasn’t a problem, as long as you kept talking. She said that in the oral, in 2027, she had stopped in the middle of a sentence, unable to find a word. The silence lasted so long that the examiner thought she had finished. Then Ioana took a breath and carried on, with another word. She told Haruka that if it happened to her tomorrow, she should think of the waltz. A silence wasn’t an end. It was a pause before what came next.

Before leaving, Inès gave Haruka one last piece of advice. She said the best way to write an argumentative text was to imagine a real person in front of you. Not an examiner, not a jury: a real person you wanted to convince. She said she herself always thought of her mother, coming home from the hospital in the morning, tired, with no time to read complicated sentences. Haruka asked who she should think of. Inès said: “Your grandmother.”

Around ten everyone went home. Haruka stayed on the landing for a while, between the two doors, as she often did now. She took out her violin. She played the waltz very softly, up to the silence of the third verse. She stopped. Eight bars. She counted in her head. On the fifth, on the other side of Julien’s door, someone struck a saucepan once, like a triangle. It was Rose-Hélène. Haruka burst out laughing and finished the waltz.

On Saturday 13 December Haruka woke at six, before her alarm. She opened the shutters. Outside, everything was white. It had snowed all night over Lyon. The roofs, cars and trees of the rue d’Austerlitz were covered in a thick, silent layer. Not a sound in the street. Not a car. Only the snow, still falling slowly in big flakes. Haruka stood at the window for a long time. She thought the city itself had decided to be silent for her.

On her phone there were messages. Aoi, from Kyoto, where it was already half past twelve, with a video: the university waltz club, sixty students, wishing her luck in French with a terrible accent. Her grandmother, in the same video, giving a thumbs-up. Hortense Valmont, who had written a single line: “Don’t look for who it is. Answer.” As for Farid, whom she didn’t know yet, he was of course not among her messages. She would meet him two hours later.

At half past seven she went down to Gérard’s café with Isabelle. She wasn’t hungry, but Isabelle had insisted. The café was open despite the snow. Gérard was waiting for her behind the counter. He had made green tea in Odile’s cup, the one with the little blue flower. And around the table by the window sat the six members of the op-ed club, who had come specially through the snow at half past seven on a Saturday morning to wish her luck.

The old Latin teacher shook her hand very solemnly. He said a sentence to her in Latin, which he translated at once: “Fortune favours the bold.” The night nurse gave her a croissant. The delivery driver gave her a new pen, just in case. Gérard said nothing. He just put his hand on her shoulder for a second, the way you do with someone setting off on a journey. Haruka drank her tea. She ate half the croissant. Then she set off through the snow with Isabelle towards the Alliance française.

In the street the snow crunched under their feet. There was hardly anyone about. The trams weren’t running yet. The few passers-by walked slowly and carefully, leaving tracks in the fresh snow. Haruka said she had never heard Lyon so quiet. Isabelle said her mother had loved snowy mornings, because they were the only times you could hear the city breathe. Haruka thought it might be a sign. She didn’t believe in signs. That morning she decided to believe.

In the exam room there were thirty-two candidates. Haruka looked at them as she sat down. There was a Brazilian student who wanted to study medicine, a Ukrainian nurse who wanted her qualification recognised, a Chinese engineer, a young Colombian woman, two Italians, an American married to a Lyonnais. And next to her a boy of about twenty, thin and very pale, holding his pen with both hands so it wouldn’t shake. His name was Farid. He came from Afghanistan.

The invigilator, a woman of about fifty with short hair, read out the instructions. Phones switched off and placed on the table by the door. No dictionaries. No talking between candidates. A black or blue pen. Haruka put on the desk in front of her Odile’s pencil, Jeanne Valmont’s bookmark and the delivery driver’s new pen. Farid looked at the three objects with curiosity. He asked in a whisper whether they were lucky charms. Haruka said yes. He took a small round stone from his pocket. He said: “Me too.”

The first paper was listening comprehension. The loudspeakers spat out a few seconds of noise, then a woman’s voice announced the first document. It was an interview with an acoustics expert about noise in cities. Haruka read the questions before listening, as Isabelle had taught her. She underlined the keywords. During the first listening she wrote nothing. During the second she noted words in the margin. She didn’t panic. At one point she even understood one of the expert’s jokes and smiled.

The second audio document, played only once, was harder: a report on a bakers’ strike in Marseille, with interviews of angry customers all talking at once in southern accents. Haruka didn’t understand everything. She understood that the bakers were protesting about the price of flour and that customers were divided. She remembered Inès’s advice: never leave a box empty. She answered every question. For two of them, she guessed.

The second paper was reading comprehension. Two texts. The first, an article about community gardens in cities. The second, an op-ed about remote working. Haruka skimmed them in four minutes. In the op-ed, the first paragraph said remote working was a wonderful revolution. Haruka looked for the turn. It was at the start of the second paragraph: “Yet this freedom comes at a price.” The thesis was there. She smiled, thinking of Hortense and Rose-Hélène. The real message came after the “but”.

There was also a trap, exactly the one Hortense had told her about. One question said: “True or false? The author thinks remote working isolates employees.” In the text there was the sentence: “Some sociologists believe remote working isolates employees.” Haruka nearly answered “true”. Then she reread it. It wasn’t the author who thought so: it was “some sociologists”. The author said further on that it wasn’t so simple. She wrote “false” and copied out the exact sentence.

At the break there were ten minutes before the writing paper. The candidates went out into the corridor. Farid stayed in his seat, head in his hands. Haruka went over. She asked if he was all right. He said, in hesitant but correct French, that he had understood nothing of the second audio document and was going to fail. He wanted to train as a nurse. Without the DELF he couldn’t enrol. He had left his country three years before. He had taught himself French in a hostel, from library books.

Haruka sat down beside him. She gave him half her rice cake, the one her grandmother had sent from Kyoto. She told him about her first mock exam, eleven out of twenty-five, her tears, and Henri-Ion whistling outside her door. She told him you were allowed to miss one document. There were others. You just had to keep going. Farid looked at her. He asked how long she had been in France. She said: “Two and a half months.” He said he would never have believed it.

That was when Haruka realised. She had just comforted someone in French. For five minutes, without searching for words, without translating, without thinking. She had found the right words at the right moment for someone who needed them. She thought of Odile, who had whistled on the other side of a landing for a young Romanian woman who felt alone. She thought that this, in the end, was all language was for. The invigilator called the candidates back. The break was over.

The invigilator handed out the writing papers face down. She announced: “You may turn over your paper. You have one hour.” Thirty-two sheets turned at the same moment, with a sound like wind through dead leaves. Haruka read the topic. She had to read it again, because she thought she was mistaken. Then she had to stop herself laughing, alone in the middle of the silent room. Farid looked at her anxiously. She put her hand over her mouth.

The topic was: “Many people complain about the constant noise in our cities. In your opinion, does silence still have a place in our societies? You are writing on the forum of a major newspaper to give your reasoned opinion. Two hundred and fifty words minimum.” Haruka read the instructions a third time. Who is writing? Her. To whom? Readers of a forum. What for? To give her opinion and convince. She took Odile’s pencil. She opened her rough draft.

She made her plan in nine minutes. A small rectangle for the introduction. Three big rectangles. In the first she wrote: “Silence to think — library — La Duchère media library.” In the second: “Silence to listen to others — Japanese word ma — the space between two notes.” In the third: “Admittedly, noise is life — but it mustn’t replace listening.” A small rectangle for the conclusion: “Silence has become rare, therefore precious.” She looked at the clock. Fifty-one minutes left.

Before writing, she hesitated. She wanted to tell the whole story: the landing, Odile, the waltz, the eight bars, the Place des Terreaux, the forty-three boats around Yves. She had so much to say about silence. Then she remembered Hortense’s remark about houses with too many doors. She remembered Odile, who said things simply. She decided to keep the story to herself. She would leave only a trace of it, discreet, that nobody else would see.

She began to write. The first sentence came by itself: “Horns, notifications, music in shops: our cities are never silent.” A long sentence, then a short one. Then the central question, then the announcement of the plan. In the first paragraph she wrote about the Jeanne-Valmont media library, where young people from La Duchère came looking for the silence they couldn’t find at home. In the second she explained the word “ma”: the emptiness that isn’t empty, the interval that gives music its meaning.

She didn’t mention the waltz. She thought about it throughout the second paragraph, but she didn’t mention it. Inès had told her a good example had to be understandable by any reader, and nobody on the jury would know Odile’s story. So she wrote only: “In some musical traditions, the musicians all stop together in the middle of a piece for a few bars. This shared silence is not an emptiness: it is an invitation to answer.” She smiled as she wrote it. Nobody else could know.

In the third paragraph she nuanced, as Julien had taught her. “Admittedly, noise is part of urban life: it is the sound of markets, children and conversations. But it must not replace the moments when we truly listen.” Then the conclusion. She wrote it eleven minutes early, as Inès had advised, so as not to run out of time. The last sentence came to her all at once, like a violin phrase: “It remains to be seen whether we will have the courage to fall silent, and above all to listen to what comes after.”

She counted her words using Amina’s method. Three lines, an average of eleven words, twenty-six lines. Two hundred and eighty-six words. Then she reread. Once for meaning: did everything flow? Yes. A second time looking only for the five mistakes on Julien’s list. She found three. “Une idée intéressant”: she added an “e”. “Les phrases que j’ai écrit”: she added “es”. “Il est a la fois”: she put an accent on the “a”. Two minutes left.

As she reread, she heard the ticking of the clock above the board. She hadn’t noticed it while writing. Now it seemed enormous. She thought of Rose-Hélène and her timer, her station master’s voice. She smiled. She checked the opening one last time: she was writing on a forum, so no “Madame, Monsieur”, but a title and a hook. She had a title: “Silence, a luxury to protect”. She underlined it twice.

She put down her pen. She looked out of the window. Snow was still falling on Lyon, slow and silent. Next to her, Farid was still writing, very fast, bent over his sheet, his face focused. He was no longer shaking. Haruka thought of her grandmother in Kyoto, who was thinking of her at that very moment, as she had promised in her letter. She thought of Odile, who had never taken a French exam in her life, and yet had taught Ioana everything that mattered.

The invigilator announced the end of the paper. The candidates handed in their papers. Outside in the corridor Farid came over to Haruka. He was smiling for the first time that morning. He said he had written three hundred words and talked about his village in Afghanistan, where the silence of the mountains was so deep you could hear the snow fall. Haruka said that was surely the most beautiful example in the whole room. Farid said hers, about the Japanese word, was more beautiful. He had looked over her shoulder.

Handing in her paper, the American married to a Lyonnais said loudly in the corridor that the topic was absurd, because nobody could have silence in a city. The Brazilian replied that in Brazil it was even worse. The Chinese engineer said he had written about libraries. The Ukrainian nurse said nothing. She just looked at the snow through the corridor window. Haruka thought that everyone in that room had written about a different silence. And that perhaps that was the real topic.

Isabelle was waiting for her outside, in the snow, with an umbrella and a flask of tea. Haruka told her the topic. Isabelle laughed so loudly that passers-by turned round. She said that if someone had wanted to invent a topic for Haruka, they couldn’t have found a better one. They walked together to Gérard’s café for lunch. The oral began at three o’clock. Three hours left. The longest, said Haruka. Isabelle said that in the oral she wouldn’t be alone. Haruka didn’t understand what she meant.

A model text for the writing paper: a contribution to a newspaper forum. Notice the introduction, paragraphs, connectors and conclusion. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end, answer 4 questions.
Forum : faut-il interdire les téléphones portables au lycée ?

For some years now, more and more countries have banned mobile phones in schools. We may wonder whether this measure is really effective. We will first look at its advantages, then its limits, before proposing a solution.

First of all, the ban encourages concentration. Indeed, a pupil who receives a notification every five minutes cannot follow a lesson. For example, several studies show that results improve when phones stay in bags.

Moreover, it allows human contact to be restored. During breaks, instead of looking at their screens, young people talk to each other, play, and sometimes argue. That is how they learn to live together.

Admittedly, the phone can also be a teaching tool: dictionaries, research, language apps. But a total ban deprives teachers of these possibilities. It also risks being badly received by pupils, who will get round it.
That is why an intermediate solution seems preferable to me: ban phones during breaks and in class, except when the teacher decides to use them for a specific activity.
In short, the question is not whether to be for or against technology, but to learn to use it at the right moment. It remains to be seen whether adults themselves will set the example.

Horns, notifications, music in shops: our cities are never silent. We may therefore wonder whether silence still has a place in our lives.
First of all, silence is necessary for thinking. Indeed, it is hard to concentrate in noise. For example, many students work in libraries.
Moreover, silence brings us closer to others. In Japanese, the word “ma” refers to the space between two sounds, which gives meaning to what surrounds it.
Admittedly, noise is part of urban life. But it must not replace the moments when we listen.
In short, silence has not disappeared: it has become rare, and therefore precious. It remains to be seen whether we will have the courage to protect it.
